column2: follow-up question (asked when this keyPoint is uncertain; must not contain the answer)
Starting at the surface and going down, describe each layer of the Earth and which parts make up the rigid outer shell.
Why do we say the ground beneath our feet is slowly moving, and what large features come from that movement?
What drives the slow drift of continents from deep inside the Earth?
What kind of landscape results when two continents collide, and what happens when two plates pull apart under an ocean?
What kind of boundary produces mainly ground-shaking without making new crust or mountains?
List the landforms and events that come from the slow drifting of the Earth's rigid slabs.
Looking at a map of earthquakes and volcanoes beside a plate map, what pattern do you see and why would it help planners?
After a rock cracks into pieces and the pieces just lie where they fell, which process has acted and which has not?
A tree root splits a boulder, rainwater dissolves a limestone cliff and daily heat and cold crack a desert rock. Which kind of weathering is each?
Explain the difference between rocks breaking up on the spot and the broken material being carried off, and name the carriers.
A village on a riverbank loses fields and houses every monsoon. Which occupations and properties are affected and how?
What are the five natural agents that keep reshaping the land, and what do they do to hills and low ground over time?
Follow a river from its mountain source to the sea and name the typical landforms at each stage.
Why do many people settle on river deltas even though they flood, and how does a delta form?
Trace how a rocky point jutting into the sea is slowly turned into an isolated rock pillar by the waves.
What shapes remain in a mountain valley after a glacier has retreated, and what happens to the rock and debris it carried?
Which landforms would you expect in a sandy desert, and which in a region of soluble rock with acidic groundwater?
After days of heavy rain, a hillside where trees were cut and a road was built gives way. Explain the natural and human causes together.
Why might a mountain slope that held snow for weeks suddenly slide after one warm afternoon or a vibration?
What chain of events can turn a quiet high-altitude lake into a flood that devastates a valley far below?
Why do some regions get blinded by dust storms while others do not, and how can people make it worse?
Which forces build the highest peaks and which wear them down again, and why do people care about both?
